newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea threatens action as murder mystery unfolds.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea threatens action as murder mystery unfolds.

text.p: North Korea warned of "serious consequences" on Wednesday over a submarine incident, and the killing of a South Korean diplomat in Russia led to media speculation it was making good on previous threats.
Separately, South Korea's defence minister said Seoul should prepare for all-out war from North Korea. His comments were not new, but they added to a sense of alarm.

Pyongyang's latest warning was delivered in a border meeting between North Korean army officers and representatives of the U.S.-led United Nations Command, which monitors a ceasefire that ended the 1950-53 Korean war.
South Korean troops have either killed or found the bodies of 22 North Korean soldiers who landed by submarine on a South Korean beach two weeks ago.
North Korean officers "indicated that serious consequences, which would be announced, would occur as a result of the deaths of their soldiers", a U.N. Command statement said.
Earlier, the foreign ministry said a South Korean diplomat specialising in North Korean affairs was bludgeoned to death in Russia's Far East city of Vladivostok on Tuesday.
The Seoul media instantly speculated Pyongyang was behind the killing, noting South Korean diplomats were on extra alert following previous Pyongyang threats over the boat incident.
Pyongyang had threatened to retaliate "a hundredfold or a thousandfold".
Foreign ministry spokesman Suh Dae-won declined comment on the speculation surrounding the death of Choi Duck-keun.
"He was killed on the stairs of his apartment building by unidentified men," Suh said.
"What we know officially from our investigations is that he was hit on the head by a very heavy tool," he said. His wallet, passport, cash and other personal belongings were untouched.
Vladivostok Consul General Lee Suk-gon told South Korean television in a telephone interview that there was no evidence Pyongyang had a hand in the slaying.
"We presume it was a planned and pre-organised murder but it is hard for us to conclude that North Korea did it because there is no evidence," Lee said.
Defence minister Lee Yang-ho said South Korea must be ready for the worst.

"In the worst case, we may have to be prepared for an all-out war, with North Korea deploying long range artillery pieces, including Scud missiles," a ministry official quoted him as telling a parliamentary committee.
"The North could wage limited military provocations or a blitzkrieg when Kim Jong-il faces a political crisis or miscalculates the current situation," Lee said, referring to the North Korean leader.
Pyongyang maintains the submarine drifted into Southern waters after developing engine trouble.

South Korea insists it was a commando operation in preparation for wider military action. A total of 26 North Koreans are thought to have come ashore, and an intense search is underway for three still missing.
South Korean President Kim Young-sam ordered Lee to ensure the armed forces are fully ready to deal with any North Korean provocation, a presidential spokesman said.
Following the killing of the envoy South Korea instructed overseas missions to guard against possible terrorist attacks, a foreign ministry official said.

Vladivostok has a reputation for mafia-style gangs and lawlessness. Several South Korean trading and shipping companies operate in the port city, and a number of North Koreans are also stationed there.
